questions.stem: In which three countries is German the main official language?
questions.explanation: German is official in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and also in Liechtenstein and part of Belgium. Switzerland has four official languages, of which German is the most widely spoken.

questions.stem: Roughly how many people speak German as a first language?
questions.explanation: Around 95 million, which makes it the most widely spoken first language in the European Union — ahead of French, Italian and Spanish within Europe itself.

questions.stem: What is „Hochdeutsch“?
options: An old form of German no longer used
A formal greeting used in Austria
Standard German, used in writing and broadcasting
The German spoken in the mountains
questions.explanation: 'High German' refers to the standard form, not to altitude or status. Regional dialects remain strong, and a Bavarian and a Hamburger speaking broad dialect can struggle to understand each other.

questions.stem: Which greeting suits a teacher you have just met?
questions.explanation: „Guten Tag“ with a surname is the safe formal greeting. „Hallo“ and „na?“ are for friends, and using them with a teacher would read as over-familiar.

questions.stem: What does choosing „Sie“ rather than „du“ signal?
options: Respect or distance with someone you do not know well
That the sentence is in the past tense
That you are talking to more than one person
questions.explanation: English lost this distinction when 'thou' fell out of use. Germans are still offered the switch explicitly — being invited to „duzen“ someone is a small social event.

questions.stem: Why is „Sie“ meaning 'you' always capitalised?
options: Because all pronouns are capitalised in German
Because it is a formal title
It is only capitalised at the start of a sentence
To tell it apart from „sie“ meaning she or they
questions.explanation: „Sie“, „sie“ and „sie“ are the same three letters for 'you', 'she' and 'they'. The capital is the only thing separating the formal 'you' in writing — in speech, context does the work.

questions.stem: Why does German capitalise every noun?
options: It marks the subject of the sentence
It shows the noun is plural
It is a spelling convention that marks nouns wherever they appear
Only nouns for people are capitalised
questions.explanation: German is the only major language that capitalises all nouns. It is genuinely useful for a reader: you can pick the nouns out of a long sentence before you understand any of it.

questions.stem: What is a 'false friend' in language learning?
options: A word borrowed directly from another language
A word with more than one meaning
A word that is hard to pronounce
A word that looks the same in two languages but means something else
questions.explanation: „Gift“ means poison in German. „Bekommen“ means to receive, not to become. False friends are dangerous precisely because they look easy.

questions.stem: What does the German word „Gift“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Das Gift“ is poison. The English 'gift' is „das Geschenk“. It is the best-known false friend between the two languages and worth meeting early.

questions.stem: What does „bekommen“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Bekommen“ is to get or receive; 'to become' is „werden“. „Ich bekomme ein Buch“ means you are given one, not that you are turning into one.

questions.stem: Which English word came from German?
questions.explanation: Kindergarten, rucksack, delicatessen and angst all came from German. English and German share a Germanic root, which is why so much core vocabulary — house/Haus, water/Wasser, book/Buch — looks familiar.

questions.stem: What is a cognate?
options: A word spelled the same but pronounced differently
A word that looks similar in two languages and shares its meaning
A word with no translation in the other language
questions.explanation: „Haus“, „Wasser“, „Finger“ and „Hand“ are cognates with English. German and English are closely related, so a German text is far less opaque to an English speaker than it first looks.

questions.stem: How does German build long words like „Handschuh“?
options: It shortens a phrase and drops the vowels
It joins existing nouns together into one word
It adds endings to a verb
questions.explanation: „Handschuh“ is hand + shoe, meaning glove. German compounds freely, which is why its longest words look alarming and are usually just three ordinary nouns stuck together.

questions.stem: Why does German need cases where English mostly does not?
options: Cases show a word's role, which lets the word order move
German has no word order rules at all
Cases only exist in written German
English lost cases in the twentieth century
questions.explanation: English marks roles by position — 'the dog bites the man' versus 'the man bites the dog'. German marks them on the article, so it can move phrases for emphasis without losing who did what.

questions.stem: Which statement about German in Australia is accurate?
options: It is one of the languages taught in Australian schools
It is an official language of Australia
It is spoken as a first language by most Australians
It is taught only at university level
questions.explanation: German is offered in many Australian schools alongside Japanese, Italian, Chinese, Indonesian and French. Australia has no official language declared in law at all.

questions.stem: What does it mean that German is pluricentric?
options: It has a formal and an informal register
Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have accepted standard forms
It has more than one writing system
It is spoken on several continents
questions.explanation: Austrian and Swiss Standard German differ from German Standard German in vocabulary and usage — an Austrian says „Jänner“ where a German says „Januar“. None is a mistake, in the same way Australian English is not incorrect British.

questions.stem: Which of these countries has German as its main official language?
questions.explanation: Germany, Austria and Switzerland are the three main ones. Liechtenstein uses German too, and it is one of four official languages in Switzerland.

questions.stem: What is the capital of Austria?
questions.explanation: Vienna, or „Wien“ in German. Salzburg is smaller and better known for Mozart.

questions.stem: What is the capital of Germany?
questions.explanation: Berlin became the capital again after reunification in 1990. Bonn had been the West German capital before that.

questions.stem: Which city is the capital of Switzerland?
questions.explanation: Zurich is the largest city and Geneva the most international, but Bern holds the federal government.

questions.stem: Which greeting would you use with a friend?
questions.explanation: „Hallo“ is informal. „Guten Tag“ is the neutral daytime greeting and „auf Wiedersehen“ is a farewell.

questions.stem: Which greeting is common in southern Germany and Austria?
questions.explanation: „Grüß Gott“ is standard in Bavaria and Austria. „Moin“ belongs to the north, which shows how regional German greetings are.

questions.stem: What does „Tschüss“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Tschüss“ is an informal goodbye. „Auf Wiedersehen“ is the formal one.

questions.stem: What does „Bitte“ mean when you hand something over?
questions.explanation: „Bitte“ covers please, you are welcome and here you are. Context does all the work.

questions.stem: What is the usual reply to „Danke“?
questions.explanation: „Bitte“ or „Bitte schön“. The same word that asks politely also answers thanks.

questions.stem: What does „Entschuldigung“ mean?
questions.explanation: It works both for apologising and for getting someone's attention, like 'excuse me' in English.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „Chef“ mean?
questions.explanation: A cook is „der Koch“. German took „Chef“ from French, where it means head or chief.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „Rat“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Ein guter Rat“ is good advice. The animal is „die Ratte“, with two t's.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „Handy“ mean in German?
questions.explanation: It looks English and is not used this way in English at all — German invented the usage.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „also“ mean in German?
questions.explanation: 'Also' in English is „auch“. The two words are spelt identically and mean different things.

questions.stem: What does „bald“ mean in German?
questions.explanation: „Bis bald“ means see you soon. Having no hair is „kahl“.

questions.stem: Which English word was borrowed from German?
questions.explanation: Cafe and ballet are French, piano is Italian. Kindergarten, angst and delicatessen are also German borrowings.

questions.stem: What does „Kindergarten“ mean literally?
questions.explanation: Friedrich Froebel coined it in 1840. English borrowed the word whole, compound and all.

questions.stem: What does the German habit of compounding produce?
options: Long single words built from shorter ones
questions.explanation: „Handschuh“ is hand plus shoe, meaning glove. English would write two words or hyphenate.

questions.stem: What gender does a German compound noun take?
options: The gender of its first part
The gender of its last part
questions.explanation: „Der Handschuh“ is masculine because „der Schuh“ is. The last element decides.

questions.stem: What is the currency of Germany and Austria?
questions.explanation: Both adopted the euro in 2002. Switzerland kept the Swiss franc.

questions.stem: How are dates written in German?
questions.explanation: „Der 3. März“ — the day number takes a full stop, which marks it as an ordinal.

questions.stem: Why does „3.“ have a full stop in a German date?
options: It shows the date is approximate
questions.explanation: The stop is how German writes 'third' rather than 'three'. English uses -rd instead.

questions.stem: What is „das Abitur“?
questions.explanation: It is the qualification for university entry, roughly equivalent in purpose to the VCE.

questions.stem: What is „die Lehre“ in the German education system?
questions.explanation: The dual system combines paid work with classroom study and is a mainstream route rather than a fallback.

questions.stem: At what time does the German school day usually end?
questions.explanation: Traditional German schools finish around one o'clock, though all-day schools are becoming more common.

questions.stem: What does „Guten Morgen“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Guten Morgen“, „Guten Tag“ and „Guten Abend“ divide the day. „Gute Nacht“ is only said at bedtime.

questions.stem: Why is the „Sie“ meaning 'you' always capitalised?
options: To distinguish it from sie meaning she or they
questions.explanation: Without the capital, „sie“ could be she, they or formal you. In speech the verb ending helps instead.

questions.stem: Which statement about „du“ and „Sie“ is accurate?
options: Sie is only used in writing
Du is the plural of Sie
Using du with a stranger can seem over-familiar
Du is used with everyone in Germany
questions.explanation: Young people use „du“ with each other readily, but an adult stranger or a teacher expects „Sie“.

questions.stem: What does it mean to be invited to „duzen“ someone?
options: To move to first names and du
questions.explanation: It marks a real shift in the relationship, and the older or more senior person usually offers it.

questions.stem: What is „Schweizerdeutsch“?
options: The German taught in Swiss schools
questions.explanation: Swiss German is spoken while standard German is written, so a learner can read everything and still struggle to follow a conversation.

questions.stem: Which letter does Swiss German writing not use?
questions.explanation: Switzerland writes „ss“ where Germany writes „ß“. The umlauts are used everywhere.

questions.stem: What does the letter ß represent?
questions.explanation: It is called „Eszett“ or „scharfes S“ and only ever appears in lowercase, after a long vowel or a diphthong.

questions.stem: What do the two dots of an umlaut do?
questions.explanation: „Mutter“ and „Mütter“ differ only in those dots, and mean mother and mothers. They are not decoration.

questions.stem: How is ä written when umlauts are unavailable?
questions.explanation: ä, ö and ü become ae, oe and ue, and ß becomes ss. You still see this in email addresses and web domains.

questions.stem: What does „Danke schön“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Schön“ adds warmth. The reply is „Bitte schön“.

questions.stem: What is „das Oktoberfest“?
questions.explanation: It runs from late September into early October despite the name, and Munich is its home.

questions.stem: What is celebrated on 3 October in Germany?
options: The start of the school year
The end of the First World War
questions.explanation: „Tag der Deutschen Einheit“ marks reunification in 1990 and is the national holiday.

questions.stem: What was the Berlin Wall?
options: A border between Germany and Poland
A barrier dividing the city from 1961 to 1989
questions.explanation: It separated East and West Berlin for twenty-eight years, and its fall led to reunification within a year.

questions.stem: What does „die Autobahn“ refer to?
questions.explanation: Parts of the network have no general speed limit, which is why the word is known internationally.

questions.stem: Which meal is „das Frühstück“?
questions.explanation: „Mittagessen“ is lunch and „Abendessen“ dinner. „Abendbrot“, literally evening bread, is the lighter cold version.

questions.stem: What is „Abendbrot“?
options: A cold evening meal of bread and toppings
A large cooked dinner eaten late at night
A sweet snack taken in the afternoon
A cake served with coffee on Sundays
questions.explanation: The main hot meal is traditionally at midday, which is why the evening one can be cold.

questions.stem: What does „Gesundheit“ literally mean, said to someone who sneezes?
questions.explanation: It literally means health, and is used where English says 'bless you'. English borrowed the word itself rather than translating it.

questions.stem: Which statement about German dialects is accurate?
options: They vary enough to hinder mutual understanding
questions.explanation: A Bavarian and a speaker from Hamburg may switch to standard German to be sure of each other.

questions.stem: Which word differs between German and Austrian standard German?
questions.explanation: Germany says „Kartoffel“ and Austria „Erdapfel“. Everyday food words vary the most.

questions.stem: Why is German useful for studying science and engineering?
options: A large body of research has been published in it
It is the official language of science
questions.explanation: German was a dominant language of research for much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

questions.stem: Why do English and German share so many basic words?
options: The two were once the same language
Both descend from the same Germanic ancestor
questions.explanation: Hand, finger, water, house and come are all shared inheritance rather than borrowing.

questions.stem: What does „Fernweh“ describe?
options: A longing to travel far away
questions.explanation: It is the mirror image of „Heimweh“, homesickness. English has no single word for it.

questions.stem: What does „Schadenfreude“ mean?
questions.explanation: Borrowed into English whole, because English had the idea and no word for it.

questions.stem: What is „die Weihnachtszeit“?
questions.explanation: German Christmas markets open in late November, and the main celebration is on Christmas Eve rather than Christmas Day.

questions.stem: When do German families traditionally exchange presents?
questions.explanation: „Der Heilige Abend“ is the main evening. In Australia the exchange is usually the following morning.

questions.stem: Why might a German speaker seem blunt to an Australian?
options: German speakers dislike small talk rules
German has no word for please
questions.explanation: Directness is read as honesty rather than rudeness. The language has a full set of politeness forms.

questions.stem: What does „Feierabend“ mean?
options: The end of the working day
questions.explanation: Literally 'celebration evening'. It names the moment work stops, which says something about how the boundary is regarded.

questions.stem: What is „das Pfand“ on a drink bottle?
options: The name of the bottling company
The date by which it should be drunk
A deposit refunded when you return it
A tax charged on imported drinks
questions.explanation: Germany's deposit scheme returns money at a machine in the supermarket, which is why return rates are so high.

questions.stem: What does „Mahlzeit“ do?
questions.explanation: Literally 'mealtime', used as a greeting in workplaces near midday. English has nothing equivalent.

questions.stem: Which is the polite way to order in a German cafe?
questions.explanation: „Ich hätte gern“ or „Ich möchte“ soften the request. „Ich will“ is grammatical and blunt.

questions.stem: Why is learning set phrases whole useful in German?
options: Some cannot be assembled from the rules
questions.explanation: „Es gibt“, „Wie geht's“ and „zu Hause“ each behave in ways the grammar rules alone would not predict.

questions.stem: What does „Es gibt“ literally say?
questions.explanation: The literal sense explains why the noun after it is an accusative object rather than a subject.
